title: Jeremiah 10:17–25
context: The unit opens with a call to those under siege to gather their belongings (10:17), followed by the LORD’s word that he will “sling out” the inhabitants (10:18). A first-person lament follows (10:19–20); many read it as Jeremiah voicing the grief of the land, and others hear Jerusalem herself speaking as a mother whose children are gone. The voice blames the shepherds who did not inquire of the LORD (10:21) and hears news of an invader from the north (10:22). The unit closes in prayer (10:23–25). On how God directs human steps (10:23), see the existing boxes at Proverbs 16:9 and Proverbs 20:24 rather than a new one. The closing plea in 10:25 closely parallels Psalm 79:6–7; the two are named without harmonizing.

verses.text: Gather up your wares out of the land, you who live under siege.
verses.arminianNotes: Those under siege are told to gather their wares out of the land. Arminian readers see an urgent warning to prepare for exile, as the judgment so often announced draws near.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the command as signaling that the threatened siege and deportation are now certain. Both traditions read the verse as a sudden shift from hymn to crisis, bringing the coming invasion close to home.

verses.text: For the LORD says, “Behold, I will sling out the inhabitants of the land at this time, and will distress them, that they may feel it.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will sling out the inhabitants of the land and distress them so they may feel it. Arminian readers note the purpose clause: God wants the people to feel the reality of their condition, perhaps to awaken them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sling image as the LORD’s decisive act in judgment, hurling the people into exile. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as God’s own announcement of judgment, meant to be felt and not ignored.

verses.text: Woe is me because of my injury! My wound is serious; but I said, “Truly this is my grief, and I must bear it.”
verses.arminianNotes: A voice cries woe over its serious wound, yet resolves to bear its grief. Arminian readers note the acceptance in the line: the speaker owns the suffering rather than denying it, perhaps the prophet speaking for the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the speaker, whether Jeremiah or personified Jerusalem, submitting to judgment as from God’s hand. Both traditions read the resolve to bear the grief as a step toward honest acceptance, without settling the speaker’s identity.

verses.text: My tent has been destroyed, and all my cords are broken. My children have gone away from me, and they are no more. There is no one to spread my tent any more, to set up my curtains.
verses.arminianNotes: The speaker’s tent is destroyed, the cords broken, and the children gone, with no one to set up the curtains. Arminian readers see the image of a household broken apart, a picture of the land emptied by exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the tent and children may picture Jerusalem as a mother bereft of her people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as heartbreaking imagery of loss, handled gently and without forcing the identification.

verses.text: For the shepherds have become brutish, and have not inquired of the LORD. Therefore they have not prospered, and all their flocks have scattered.
verses.arminianNotes: The shepherds have become brutish and have not inquired of the LORD, so the flocks are scattered. Arminian readers see leaders responsible for failing to seek God, whose neglect harmed the people under their care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the shepherds as Judah’s rulers, whose failure to inquire of the LORD brought ruin. Both traditions read the verse as a sobering word about the accountability of leaders, a theme Jeremiah develops later (compare 23:1–4).

verses.text: The voice of news, behold, it comes, and a great commotion out of the north country, to make the cities of Judah a desolation, a dwelling place of jackals.
verses.arminianNotes: News comes of a great commotion from the north to make Judah’s cities a desolation and a home for jackals. Arminian readers note that the long-announced northern threat is now heard approaching.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the invader from the north, often identified with Babylon, as the instrument of God’s judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the fulfillment of earlier warnings (compare 1:13–15), with the identification held loosely.

verses.text: LORD, I know that the way of man is not in himself. It is not in man who walks to direct his steps.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah confesses that the way of man is not in himself, nor can he direct his own steps. Arminian readers see humility before God: people need divine guidance and grace, while still making real choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence governing human paths. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as dependence on God; on how divine direction and human choice relate, see the existing keyContrasts at Proverbs 16:9 and Proverbs 20:24.

verses.text: LORD, correct me, but gently; not in your anger, lest you reduce me to nothing.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah asks the LORD to correct him gently, not in anger, lest he be reduced to nothing. Arminian readers see a plea for discipline that restores rather than destroys, offered on behalf of himself and his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prayer as accepting God’s correction while appealing to his mercy. Both traditions read the verse as a humble model of prayer under discipline, seeking measured correction rather than escape from it.

verses.text: Pour out your wrath on the nations that don’t know you, and on the families that don’t call on your name; for they have devoured Jacob. Yes, they have devoured him, consumed him, and have laid waste his habitation.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah asks God to pour out wrath on nations that do not know him, for they have devoured Jacob. Arminian readers note that the request hands justice to God, and that the line closely parallels Psalm 79:6–7.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prayer as appealing to God’s justice against those who destroyed his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the plea as honest prayer in crisis, and they name the Psalm 79 parallel without harmonizing the wording.
